brief:
WHAT HAPPENED
- US President Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days, stating Tehran offered it because it is losing the war.
- A state dinner between Trump and Chinese President Xi featured warm words but resulted in little progress on key issues dividing the two nations.
- The US rejected appeals from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face leaders to set global AI risk evaluation standards.
- Heathrow Airport warned its planned third runway could face a four-year delay past the UK government's 2035 target.
- UK diesel prices neared an all-time high, reaching an average of 198.32p per litre according to the RAC.

WHY IT MATTERS
- Energy and transport costs: High fuel prices and unresolved shipping passage through the Strait of Hormuz maintain pressure on international transport networks and household budgets.
- Regulatory uncertainty: Turning down uniform AI standards means tech firms face an unclear international rulebook rather than a coordinated global framework.
- Infrastructure timelines: Delays to capital projects—large-scale investments in long-term physical assets like airport runways—can alter future commercial capacity plans.

WHAT TO WATCH TODAY
- International diplomatic and trade reactions to the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
- Follow-up commentary from US or Chinese officials after the leaders' state dinner.
- Ongoing responses from technology leaders regarding the US stance on AI safety standards.
- Statements from UK transport officials concerning Heathrow's projected runway timeline.

IN SIMPLE TERMS
Geopolitical and economic strains continue to shape the global agenda. The US rejected an Iranian proposal to unblock the critical Strait of Hormuz shipping route and dismissed calls from tech firms for shared international AI standards. Meanwhile, talks between the US and China showed diplomatic courtesy but little concrete agreement, while UK consumers face near-peak diesel prices and a likely multi-year delay to Heathrow's runway project.
